Closest: Burr. 204 claims are at or above the policy limit, so the loss was at least the claim: each counts as the probability of exceeding it (censored), not as a claim of that size. The parameters are of all claims, before the limits. The K-S distance is to the Kaplan-Meier estimate of the claim sizes, which allows for the limits; the A-D statistic needs every claim's size, so it is not given. The Pareto starts at the smallest claim, the generalised Pareto at zero.

The conditional tail expectation (CTE, also TVaR or expected shortfall) at a level is the mean claim above that percentile. The claims at their policy limits hide the sizes of the largest losses, so the claims give no CTE: the fits estimate it, from the limits as well as the claims.

How to read this report

  • Each analysis is the one last run on its tab of the tool, with the columns and options under Data and settings.
  • Frequency: the AIC weighs the fit against the number of parameters, and the lowest is the best. A zero-inflated model adds periods without a claim to a Poisson or a Negative Binomial.
  • Severity: the K-S distance is the largest gap between a fitted and the empirical cumulative distribution; the Anderson-Darling statistic weighs the tails more. For both, lower is closer. The Q-Q plot shows how the tail fits, the P-P plot the body.
  • The conditional tail expectation at a level is the mean claim above that percentile; a Hill plot that is level shows a Pareto tail, with the alpha it reads.
  • The sliced and piecewise models fit Pareto tails above the points chosen in the tool: move them there and save the report again to compare.
  • The tool's Export tab sends a fitted frequency and severity to NetSimulator, the claims simulator.
